title: Rousseau

cards.b:
Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712-78), born in Geneva, is the thinker of popular sovereignty. He inspired the French Revolution, democratic republicanism and also its critics. UPSC asks about the general will, his view of freedom and his place among the social contract thinkers.

The Discourse on Inequality (1755) and The Social Contract (1762) are the two texts most often set in UPSC answers. Rousseau also wrote Emile in 1762.

In Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755) Rousseau says the natural man is free, peaceful, and moved by self-love (amour de soi) and pity. The rise of private property and vanity (amour-propre) produced inequality, conflict and a false contract favouring the rich.

Unlike Hobbes, he thinks society, not nature, corrupts humans. Famous opening of The Social Contract (1762): 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.'
The contract is made among equals, not with a ruler. The ruler (government) is only an agent of the sovereign people.

The general will is what the people want as citizens, looking to the common good. It differs from the will of all, which is the sum of private interests. It is always right, says Rousseau, though not always enlightened, so a wise 'Legislator' may be needed.

Citizens who refuse to follow it can be 'forced to be free', meaning forced to obey the law they gave themselves.

Sovereignty is inalienable (cannot be given away), indivisible and absolute. It cannot be represented: 'The English people thinks it is free; it is mistaken; it is free only during the election of members of Parliament.' He preferred direct democracy in small states, as in Geneva or Corsica, with a civil religion to bind citizens.

Rousseau's freedom is moral self-rule: obeying a law I made. He insisted that no citizen should be rich enough to buy another, or poor enough to be forced to sell himself. His Emile (1762) proposes a natural education, and his view of women there is traditional, criticised by Wollstonecraft.

• Isaiah Berlin: 'forced to be free' is positive liberty and a route to tyranny.
  • J.L. Talmon, Origins of Totalitarian Democracy (1952), links the general will to Jacobin terror.
  • Who defines the general will? Easily claimed by a party or leader.
  • Direct democracy is hard in large states.
  • Defenders: Rousseau cares about law and rights, and about equal citizens.

Hobbes: fear of death, absolute sovereign. Locke: protect property, limited government, consent and revolution. Rousseau: community and common good, sovereign people. He moves from the individual's rights to the collective's moral freedom. Kant, Hegel and Marx all learn from him.

Rousseau wrote in 1762, more than a century after Hobbes's Leviathan (1651), and his answer to Hobbes's fear was moral freedom through the general will.

The idea of popular sovereignty is in the Preamble: 'We, the People of India'. Gandhi's village democracy and JP's participatory model have a Rousseauian flavour. Debates on referendum, recall and the Supreme Court's reading of the 'will of the people' invoke him. Mind the contrast with the Constituent Assembly's choice of representative democracy.

"Explain Rousseau's concept of the general will."
"'Man is born free and everywhere he is in chains.' Discuss."
"Compare Rousseau's social contract with those of Hobbes and Locke."

Structure: state of nature, contract, general will, sovereignty, freedom, critiques, comparison, Indian link.

The line 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains' opens Book I, chapter 1 of The Social Contract (1762), so quote it with that source.
